espinha: As visitas ao fundo da Fossa de Porto Rico, em ordem (1883, 1939, 1964, 1970, 2002–2003, 2015, dezembro de 2018, a conferência de 2019, a mesma expedição no extremo sul em 2019, e a volta de 2019 ao sítio de 1964), cada uma com o que trouxe e o que corrigiu da anterior. Dois fios visuais atravessam as partes: o MAPA DAS VISITAS (um alfinete com o ano por visita de lugar conhecido; o anel do ponto mais fundo aceso fraco desde p1, que acende de vez em p5) e o MEDIDOR DE PROFUNDIDADE (uma régua vertical em pés que ganha um marcador por visita; em p6, o número da lista cai dentro da rocha). O gancho abre dois laços que o corpo fecha: o número da lista (sementes em p1 e p3, pago em p6) e os 'peixes' de 1964 (aberto de novo em p2, pago em p8).
resumo: O ponto mais fundo do Atlântico fica a umas 83 mi de Porto Rico, a mais de 5 mi de profundidade. O vídeo conta como se soube: o arame do Blake em 1883 (lodo marrom, ~60 mi a leste), o eco do USS Milwaukee em 1939 (mais de 28.000 ft, e o nome Milwaukee Deep), a tripulação francesa do Archimède em 1964 (mais de 4 mi, sem chegar ao ponto, e um relato de uns 200 peixes), a rede de 1970 (uma enguia de profundidade desconhecida), o multifeixe do USGS em 2002–2003 (~27.300 ft, quinze anos antes de alguém chegar ao ponto) e o porquê da fossa (as placas, a gravidade, a laje, a fossa afundando), as paredes e o que o mar já levou à terra (1918 na Passagem de Mona; o tsunami de 1381–1391 em Anegada, da parte leste), o robô de 2015 na parede, o sonar da Five Deeps (~27.500 ft, ±16 ft) e Vescovo sozinho em 19/12/2018, a conferência de 2019 (a lista ~1.200 ft funda demais até pelo menos 2019, uma crista no ponto da lista, o ponto posto em águas da República Dominicana antes de a expedição o pôr em águas dos EUA), a outra candidata (o Meteor, 370 ft mais raso; a linha de 60°S; o Factorian) e, no fim, a volta de 2019 ao sítio de 1964: pepinos-do-mar onde se relataram peixes, e o ponto mais fundo do Atlântico na borda de onde, pela NOAA, os peixes param.
pergunta: So what is really down there, and how did anyone find out?
pergunta_no_gancho: S11, a última frase antes da assinatura: 'So what is really down there, and how did anyone find out?'. A pergunta não volta no fecho.
pergunta_longa: What is at the bottom of the Atlantic, about 83 miles off Puerto Rico, and how did anyone find out?

tese.frase: O ponto mais fundo do Atlântico, a umas 83 mi de Porto Rico e a uns 27.500 ft, só se conhece porque gente e máquinas foram até a fossa, uma visita depois da outra, e cada uma corrigiu o que a anterior deixou: o número de referência ficou uns 1.200 ft fundo demais até pelo menos 2019, mesmo com o sonar do USGS mostrando outra coisa desde 2003, até um levantamento no local e um mergulho o confirmarem; o ponto mudou de águas no papel antes de cair nas dos EUA; e os '200 peixes' de 1964 eram, pela conclusão de quem voltou ao mesmo sítio em 2019, pepinos-do-mar. O que há lá embaixo é um fundo na borda de onde, pela NOAA, os peixes param.
o_que_ela_nao_diz: Que a ciência mediu errado por 80 anos ou de 1939 a 2018: o USGS tinha ~27.300 ft em 2003; o que ficou errado foi o número da lista (F09, F32; N04, C21).
Que Vescovo foi o primeiro humano no fundo da fossa ou do Atlântico: o Archimède desceu na fossa em 1964; Vescovo é o primeiro a chegar ao ponto mais fundo (F39; N03, C20).
Que o Archimède pousou no fundo, quanto desceu em número, nem o mês (F36; N28, C08).
Que os franceses viram pepinos-do-mar ou que isso foi provado: é a conclusão dos autores, pela densidade e pela aparência (F38; N45).
Que o número de 1939 foi copiado para a lista (F29; N23), nem que 1883 acertou (F23; N22).
Que o tsunami medieval saiu do ponto mais fundo, que 1918 veio da fossa, ou que um grande terremoto vem aí (F46, F53, F56; N10, N11, N24).
Que o ponto fica em território dos EUA: fica na zona econômica, 'in U.S. waters off Puerto Rico' (F14, F15; N32).
Que a enguia de 1970 é o peixe mais fundo (F69; N18).
Que a Fossa das Sandwich do Sul é mais funda, ou que alguém mergulhou no Meteor (F74, F75; N14, N21).
Que o mapa do mundo (a GEBCO) já mostra o ponto da Five Deeps (F90; N49), ou que o ponto nunca tinha sido mapeado (F21; N40).
Que o nome Brownson Deep vem do comandante do Blake (F24; N09).
Que o fundo no ponto é o corredor plano de 13 × 3 km (F19; N46): a fala não descreve o fundo no ponto, porque nenhuma fonte o descreve.

promessa: Seguir, visita por visita, o que desceu à Fossa de Porto Rico e o que cada visita trouxe, até saber quão fundo é de verdade, onde fica, por que o número antigo durou, e o que de fato havia lá embaixo quando os franceses disseram ter visto peixes.

payoff.resposta: O 'what': lodo marrom (p1), uma enguia de profundidade desconhecida (p2), uma fossa que afunda entre placas que deslizam (p3), paredes com deslizamentos antigos (p4–p5), um fundo a ~27.500 ft com ±16 ft, a 83 mi de Aguadilla (p5), uma crista onde a lista punha o ponto (p6), pepinos-do-mar onde se relataram peixes e o fundo na borda da vida (p8). O 'how': cada parte é uma visita (arame, som, tripulação, rede, multifeixe, robô, sonar corrigido e um homem sozinho, conferência de mesa, a volta). Nenhum número novo no fecho.
payoff.texto_previsto_em_ingles: The scientists who went back concluded that the "fish" of 1964 were sea cucumbers. It's a conclusion drawn from the count and the look. The animals the French saw that day can't be checked again. By NOAA's estimate, no fish lives much deeper than about 27,500 feet. The net that brought up the cusk-eel in 1970 had gone down nearly that far. The deepest point in the Atlantic, about 83 miles off Puerto Rico, sits right at that edge.
payoff.onde: p8, os dois últimos parágrafos; a última frase volta às 83 mi e ao 1º título.

gancho.texto:
About 83 miles off Puerto Rico, a U.S. island, lies the deepest point in the Atlantic Ocean. It's more than five miles down. Stand Mount Everest on the bottom, and its top 1,500 feet would stick out of the water. When you think "deepest ocean," you think Mariana. But that's the Pacific, about 9,500 miles away.

In 1964, a French crew dove into the Puerto Rico Trench and reported a crowd of fish. In 2019, a submersible went back to the exact same spot. It found no fish at all. The first person to reach the deepest point itself got there only in December 2018. And for decades, the official list of undersea features gave that point a number about 1,200 feet too deep, even after sonar showed otherwise. So what is really down there, and how did anyone find out? You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of the bottom of the Atlantic begins.

O 'Only' (que dois leitores a frio acharam vazio sem comparação) ganha corpo na justaposição de S1–S2 (83 mi de uma ilha, mais de 5 mi para baixo), em p5 (a costa de Aguadilla e os mais de três milhões de pessoas) e na última frase do vídeo.

b4 · O que subiu (o 'brown ooze' veio do 'número'; 'the survey's report', do 'lugar'): 'It came back up with a sample of the seafloor and a reading of the water temperature down there. The spot was named the Milwaukee Deep, after the ship.' (F26 em disputa: 'more than 28,000 feet' vale para os três números, R04, C09; o recorde é o do F26; F27; 'north of Puerto Rico', nunca 'here': a posição do Milwaukee muda de fonte para fonte. Ainda não sabe quão fundo é de verdade.

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
On January 27, 1883, a steamer of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, the Blake, lowered a weighted wire into the sea north of Puerto Rico. Its commander was a Navy officer named Brownson, who had taken charge of the ship a few months earlier. The wire went down more than five miles before it touched bottom. That was about 60 miles east of the deepest point the sonar would later find.

It came back up with a sample of the seafloor and a reading of the water temperature down there. The survey's report for that year describes the bottom as brown ooze. At the time, that was believed to be the greatest depth a sample had ever been brought up from.

The trench itself had been found eight years earlier, by the British research ship HMS Challenger, under Captain Nares, far to the east. Its sounding there reached about 23,000 feet. The trench runs for hundreds of miles, almost parallel to Puerto Rico's north coast.

In 1939, the cruiser USS Milwaukee bounced sound off the bottom north of Puerto Rico. It reported more than 28,000 feet, a record for the Atlantic at the time. The spot was named the Milwaukee Deep, after the ship. That summer, newspapers printed the news in a bulletin from the National Geographic Society.

A sound could give a number. It couldn't show anyone what was down there.

beats: b1 · A tripulação: 'In 1964, people went down into the trench themselves. They rode in a French bathyscaphe, a deep-diving craft, called Archimède.' (F36; 'bathyscaphe' definido numa oração, sem travessão; nunca 'first' nem 'French Navy', A19. Pronúncia: ar-shee-MED; bathyscaphe, BATH-ih-skaf.)

b2 · Até onde, com a disputa dita: 'It went more than four miles down. Exactly how deep, the sources disagree. It never reached the deepest point, though.' Their account, published the next year, described them as snailfish, a family of fish.' (F37, R14: sempre com verbo de relato; a profundidade é a do relato, nunca na mesma frase que 'Archimède', 'bathyscaphe' ou '1964', que o portão alertaria [archimede].)
b4 · A promessa interna: 'Keep those fish in mind.' (paga em p8.)

b5 · 1970, a rede: 'In 1970, by the account of NOAA, the U.S. ocean and weather agency, a net hauled up from the trench brought back a small cusk-eel. A cusk-eel is a fish shaped like an eel, and this one was about eight inches long.' (F69 atribuir; NOAA definida na primeira vez (tabela 'nomes'); o nome científico fica fora.)

partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Que gente desceu na fossa em 1964, a mais de quatro milhas, sem chegar ao ponto mais fundo, e voltou com um relato de uns 200 peixes; que em 1970 uma rede trouxe um peixe de verdade, de profundidade desconhecida; e que ver um pedaço ou pescar não é medir o fundo. Guarda os peixes.

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
In 1964, people went down into the trench themselves. They rode in a French bathyscaphe, a deep-diving craft, called Archimède. It went more than four miles down. Exactly how deep, the sources disagree. It never reached the deepest point, though.

About 24,000 feet down, the French crew reported a crowd of fish. Some 200 of them, along about a mile of seafloor. Their account, published the next year, described them as snailfish, a family of fish. Keep those fish in mind.

In 1970, by the account of NOAA, the U.S. ocean and weather agency, a net hauled up from the trench brought back a small cusk-eel. A cusk-eel is a fish shaped like an eel, and this one was about eight inches long. The net had gone down nearly as deep as the deepest point of the Atlantic. No one knows, though, how deep the fish was when it swam in.

A crew could see only a small patch of the trench, and a net could only bring something up. Neither could map the floor. That took a different kind of sonar.

partes.ponte_entrada: In 2002 and 2003, the U.S. Geological Survey mapped the trench with multibeam sonar, a ship's sonar that maps the seafloor in a wide strip.

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
In 2002 and 2003, the U.S. Geological Survey mapped the trench with multibeam sonar, a ship's sonar that maps the seafloor in a wide strip. It took three cruises on a NOAA ship. By the end, those surveys showed the deepest part of the trench at about 27,300 feet. That was 15 years before anyone reached the deepest point.

Why is the trench so deep? Along it, two of Earth's plates, the giant slabs of its outer shell, mostly slide past each other, with only a little of one sinking under the other. The Caribbean plate moves east about three-quarters of an inch a year.

By the USGS's measure, the trench has the most negative gravity anomaly on Earth. Gravity there falls further below normal than anywhere else. The agency found a tilted slab of limestone that starts more than 4,000 feet above sea level. It ends about 13,000 feet below it. And it reads rotated blocks of rock deep in the trench as signs that the trench has been sinking.

On the trench's walls, its maps showed something else.

partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Que o risco tem dono (o USGS) e não tem data; que o tsunami mortal de 1918 veio de um terremoto na Passagem de Mona, fora da fossa; que a única prova de um grande terremoto da própria fossa tem uns seis séculos, na parte leste, longe do ponto mais fundo, datada pelo urânio de um coral; e que eventos assim ficam milhares de anos separados.
partes.mapa: De oeste para leste (a câmera anda, o mapa não corta). A Passagem de Mona DEMARCADA entre a Hispaniola e Porto Rico (polígono lido, ou o trecho entre as duas costas, declarado), com '1918 · NOT IN THE TRENCH'; a costa oeste de Porto Rico com a cota 'UP TO 20 FT (6.1 m) · NOAA NCEI'. A câmera corre a fossa para leste até Anegada no satélite do MapTiler (com o crédito) ou no Landsat (domínio público, sem crédito na tela): a costa norte demarcada nos ~6 mi de Bones Bight a Warner (F51, as coordenadas do mapa do artigo, CC BY 4.0, declaradas), e a parte leste da fossa acesa ao norte dela, 'EASTERN PUERTO RICO TRENCH' (as áreas de ruptura de Wei et al. 2024 só pela figura 1 de Kilbourne et al. 2025: aproximadas e declaradas). O anel do ponto mais fundo fica visível, longe a oeste, para 'far from its deepest point' se ver (a distância não vai à fala, A15). Na tela, 'ANEGADA · LESS THAN 80 MI SOUTH OF THE TRENCH' (F52).

Uma régua do tempo presa à ilha: a janela 1381–1391 estreitando-se a partir das datações (a medida do urânio) e '1492 · COLUMBUS' um século depois. Em 'thousands of years apart', a régua se alonga para milhares de anos, com o evento medieval como um ponto só e o resto vazio: a imagem da calma.

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
The USGS says those walls show many old underwater landslides, and that the risk of a landslide tsunami appears to be high.

In October 1918, an earthquake struck the Mona Passage, west of Puerto Rico. It wasn't in the trench. NOAA's tsunami database puts it at magnitude 7.1. Its tsunami ran as high as 20 feet up Puerto Rico's west coast. The quake and its tsunami killed more than 100 people.

Farther east, an island holds a sign of what the trench itself can do. Anegada is a low, flat island in the British Virgin Islands. Hundreds of coral boulders lie far inland there, along about six miles of its north shore, the side that faces the trench. Dating the coral by its uranium, a 2025 study placed the tsunami that left them sometime between 1381 and 1391. That's about a century before Columbus reached the Caribbean. The authors suspect the coral died in summer or fall.

The earthquake behind it struck the eastern part of this trench, far from its deepest point. Computer models put it at magnitude 8 or more. The scientists who dated the coral call it the only known sign that this stretch of the trench can do that. And it wasn't behind the deadly tsunami of 1918. They think quakes like that come thousands of years apart.

To see the trench's walls, you need a camera down there.

partes.titulo: A robot, a sonar and a man alone
partes.funcao: demonstrar e virar: a primeira imagem real da fossa (o robô de 2015, na parede leste); o sonar moderno que pôs o ponto a ~27.500 ft com ~16 ft de margem, a 83 mi de Aguadilla; e Vescovo sozinho, cujo submersível confirmou o número. É o centro do vídeo e o lugar da inscrição
partes.abre_com: o vídeo da NOAA, EX1502 L3 Dive 09: a parede sul escura, o ROV descendo
partes.ponte_entrada: In 2015, a NOAA robot filmed the trench's south wall, almost 20,000 feet down.
beats: b1 · O robô e o lugar: 'In 2015, a NOAA robot filmed the trench's south wall, almost 20,000 feet down. That's in the eastern part of the trench, a long way from its deepest point.' (F68 e a nota: a parede a ~6.000 m, a 19°09′N, 65°24′W; nunca o fundo nem o ponto mais fundo.)

b2 · O nome e o mergulho que parou (a frase calma da inscrição): 'The robot, Deep Discoverer, worked from NOAA's ship Okeanos Explorer, on one of a dozen robot dives that expedition made. Soon after, a problem with the robot cut this one short.' (F68 e a nota: 12 mergulhos de ROV, S33; o compensador de óleo; Okeanos à folha de pronúncia, oh-kee-AH-nohs.)

b3 · O sonar moderno, e a correção do som: 'In December 2018, the Five Deeps Expedition mapped the trench with a modern sonar. To get the sonar right, the ship lowered instruments to measure how fast sound travels at every depth, from the surface to the floor. Most of the seafloor it covered had been mapped before.' (F35, F12, F21; 'most… mapped before' do 'lugar' (14 % novos), que desfaz o 'never mapped' antes que alguém o pense, N40.)

b4 · O número, com a margem e a grade (a grade veio do 'número'): 'By the expedition's survey, the deepest point of the Atlantic is about 27,500 feet down. Give or take about 16 feet. The scientists give that margin with 95 percent confidence. They built their map as a grid of squares about 250 feet across. The results were published in 2021.' (F03, F11, F35, R02; um número por frase; a tela '8,378 ± 5 M (27,487 FT) · BONGIOVANNI ET AL. 2021'.)

b5 · O lugar e a gente (o 'lugar'): 'That point lies about 83 miles from the nearest coast of Puerto Rico, off Aguadilla, in the island's northwest. More than three million people live in Puerto Rico.' (F04, R16, N26, N35; F62, R12: nunca 'four million' nem 'citizens', N12; Aguadilla à folha, ah-gwah-DEE-yah.)

b6 · Vescovo, com o dia e a solidão (o 'spot the sonar had just mapped' veio do 'lugar'): 'On Wednesday, December 19, 2018, Victor Vescovo took a submersible called Limiting Factor down to the spot the sonar had just mapped. He made the trip alone, in a sub built to reach the bottom of any ocean. The trip down took about two and a half hours. He was the first person to reach the deepest point of the Atlantic.' (F39, F35 (o levantamento em 18 e 19/12), a nota do F80 ('full ocean depth submersible'); 19/12, nunca 21/12, N06; nunca 'first human at the bottom', N03; o alerta 'first' está decidido.)

b7 · A confirmação (o 'within about 7 feet' veio do 'número'): 'The sub's own gauges confirmed the sonar's number, within about 7 feet.' (F13: 2 m = 6,6 ft; o sonar é o número e o submersível a confirmação, nunca 'corrected', N34; o '8,376 ± 5 M' do submersível só na tela, numa batida separada da do sonar, N05.)
b8 · Ponte: 'That number was not the one in the official list.'
partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Como é a fossa de verdade (a parede filmada em 2015, longe do ponto); quanto ela tem no ponto mais fundo e com que precisão (~27.500 ft, ±~16 ft, numa grade de quadrados de ~250 ft); onde ele fica (a ~83 mi de Aguadilla, com mais de três milhões de pessoas na ilha); e quem chegou lá: Vescovo, sozinho, numa quarta-feira de dezembro de 2018, com um submersível que confirmou o sonar.
partes.mapa: O alfinete '2015 · NOAA ROBOT · SOUTH WALL' em 19°09′N, 65°24′W (leste; F68), e a câmera desce do mapa para o vídeo. Depois, a câmera voa para oeste até o anel do ponto mais fundo (F10), que acende de vez: '8,378 ± 5 M · 27,487 FT'. A linha '≈ 83 MI' sai da costa de Aguadilla (18,5130°N, 67,1145°W), com o município de Aguadilla demarcado (Census 2023, S55): a região falada. A zona econômica dos EUA em volta de Porto Rico acesa (camada eez da Marine Regions, S16; a licença da camada se confere), com 'INSIDE THE U.S. EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE' na tela (a sigla só na tela; a fala não define a zona, A20). O levantamento da Five Deeps NÃO se desenha com as grades dela (A06, R18): o rótulo 'SURVEYED DEC. 18–19, 2018' fica sobre o anel, sem área.
partes.ilustracao: Sobre o mapa, o navio com o leque do multifeixe varrendo uma faixa e uma coluna do navio ao fundo com marcas a cada profundidade ('SPEED OF SOUND, MEASURED AT EVERY DEPTH'; sem número de velocidade, que o dossiê não tem); a grade de quadrados de ~250 ft fechando-se sobre o anel, com a faixa '± 16 FT' desenhada como espessura no fundo. No medidor, o submersível em traço de engenheiro desce sozinho, com um relógio comprimido no canto ('≈ 2 H 30 MIN'), passando pelos marcadores que o vídeo já deixou ('2015 · ~20,000 FT · EAST WALL', '1964 · ~24,000 FT · REPORT', '2003 · ~27,300 FT'), sem a fala listá-los: a recapitulação é só visual. Ele para no fundo; o colchete '± 16 FT' se fecha em volta; numa batida separada, 'SUB GAUGES · 8,376 ± 5 M'. Sobre o mapa, o anel pulsa uma vez quando o submersível toca o fundo. Vescovo em card só com o nome e uma linha de legenda tirada da fonte, sem foto (não há retrato livre; identidade §5).

partes.funcao: pagar a segunda virada do gancho: o número da lista contra o do sonar; o sonar do governo que já mostrava outro fundo; a conferência de 2019 que achou o fundo sempre mais raso e uma crista no ponto da lista; o ponto que mudou de águas no papel antes da publicação de 2021; o nome que saiu da lista
partes.abre_com: a ficha da lista sobre a mesa ('MILWAUKEE DEEP · 8,740 M · GEBCO GAZETTEER') e o medidor ao lado
partes.ponte_entrada: Until at least 2019, the official list of undersea features had the Milwaukee Deep at about 28,700 feet.
beats: b1 · A lista e o jornal, lado a lado: 'Until at least 2019, the official list of undersea features had the Milwaukee Deep at about 28,700 feet. That's almost exactly what the newspapers reported in 1939.' (F28, F29, R06; nunca que um número saiu do outro, N23; o '8,740 M' e o '28,680 FT' só na tela, com a fonte e o ano.)

b2 · O tamanho do erro e o sonar que já sabia: 'The floor the sonar found is about 1,200 feet shallower. And U.S. government sonar had shown a shallower floor since 2003. As late as 2011, a press release for a planned deep-diving sub listed more than 28,000 feet.' (F09, F32, F33; R03; a 3ª frase é o exemplo do número que circulou, não o alvo: a empresa não se nomeia; sem 'still'.)

b3 · A conferência, com nome e ano: 'In 2019, two scientists, Heather Stewart and Alan Jamieson, checked the published depths against sonar data that was already public. In their check, the real floor came out shallower every time. They wrote that numbers like these had spread, uncorrected, through online sources and the scientific literature.' (F34 atribuir; 'every time' vale para os três pontos que eles conferiram; é a única causa que a fala dá para o número velho ter durado, e atribuída.)

b4 · A revelação: 'At the spot the old listing pointed to, their study found about 24,400 feet, the top of a ridge.' (F30 atribuir; o momento mais forte da parte; a voz não diz onde fica esse ponto: a posição do registro antigo 'não fecha' e fica fora da fala, nota do F29.)

b5 · O ponto que mudou de águas, na ordem certa (R31): 'Their study also put the deepest point somewhere else. Working from public data from eight older surveys, it placed that point about 36 miles west of the sonar's spot, in waters claimed by the Dominican Republic. Their study came out before the expedition's own results. Those were published in 2021, and they placed the deepest point in U.S. waters off Puerto Rico, about 100 miles from the Dominican Republic.' (F15 atribuir, F16, F14; o '8,408 M' só na tela, nunca na voz ao lado do 8.378; 'west of the sonar's spot' conserta o 'farther west' da descida, que caía depois da crista e ficava ambíguo; 'U.S. waters', nunca 'territorial waters' nem 'U.S. soil', N32; o 'long, flat strip' fica fora, N46.)

b6 · A lista hoje, datada, e o pedido dos autores: 'As of October 2026, the international list of undersea feature names no longer includes the Milwaukee Deep. The two scientists had asked for that name to fall out of use.' (F28 datar e a nota (S&J pedem que o nome saia de uso); quando e por que saiu não se diz, A03; nunca 'not recognized', que o portão reprova perto do Oceano Austral.)

b7 · A entrega dos dados, atribuída (consertada: a descida não atribuía): 'The expedition's scientists write that it handed all of its sonar data to Seabed 2030, the project to map the whole ocean floor by 2030.' (F90 atribuir; nunca que o mapa do mundo já mostra o ponto, N49, A07.)
b8 · Ponte (consertada: a descida dizia 'It also took…', e o 'It' dependia de b7, que é corte): 'The expedition also took its sonar, and its sub, to the other end of the Atlantic.'
partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Que o número de referência ficou ~1.200 ft fundo demais até pelo menos 2019, com o sonar do governo mostrando outro fundo desde 2003; que o número velho durou porque foi repetido sem conferência; que no ponto que a lista apontava há uma crista; que um estudo de 2019 pôs o ponto em águas da República Dominicana antes de a expedição publicar o dela, em águas dos EUA; e que o nome saiu da lista.
partes.mapa: A peça da parte: o 'ponto mais fundo' muda de lugar no mapa, em ordem. 1) O alfinete da lista antiga em 19°35'N, 66°30'W (F29): 'MILWAUKEE DEEP · 8,740 M · LISTED UNTIL AT LEAST 2019'; a câmera desce no relevo sombreado da GEBCO (2D; o relevo 3D da GEBCO nunca foi provado no canal) e mostra a crista: '~7,450 M · A RIDGE (STEWART & JAMIESON 2019)'. 2) O ponto da estimativa de 2019 em 19,613°N, 67,847°W ('2019 ESTIMATE · 8,408 M'), dentro da zona econômica da República Dominicana demarcada (camada eez da Marine Regions, S16). 3) O anel da Five Deeps em 19,712°N, 67,311°W, dentro da zona dos EUA (Porto Rico) demarcada, com '≈ 36 MI' entre os dois e a fronteira das zonas acesa; a linha '≈ 100 MI' até a costa dominicana (La Altagracia, S55). As duas zonas acesas são a região falada.
partes.ilustracao: O número que encolhe, no medidor: a marca '28,700 FT · THE LIST' fica ABAIXO da linha do fundo do sonar ('27,500 FT'), e o vão de '≈ 1,200 FT' se preenche de rocha: o número da lista cairia dentro do chão. Depois, sobre o mapa, o anel salta da crista para o oeste (2019) e volta para leste (2021), cada salto com a data, na ordem da R31.

The expedition's scientists write that it handed all of its sonar data to Seabed 2030, the project to map the whole ocean floor by 2030.

The expedition also took its sonar, and its sub, to the other end of the Atlantic.

fecho.forma: uma cena (a volta de 2019 ao sítio de 1964) que termina num lugar (o ponto mais fundo, na borda da vida, a 83 mi da ilha)
fecho.nao_repete_a_pergunta: Nenhuma sequência de 5 palavras da pergunta do gancho ('So what is really down there, and how did anyone find out?') nas 8 últimas frases; nem 'So' nem pergunta no fecho. O portão rodado no esqueleto não deu alerta de fecho.
fecho.nao_e_lista: Nenhuma das 8 últimas frases abre com First, Then, Next, Finally, Second, Third, A ou An; a resposta vem como cena e lugar, não como inventário das visitas (a recapitulação, se houver, é só visual, no medidor de p5).
fecho.como_paga: Paga o laço do gancho (S6–S8: o que a volta achou), a pergunta ('what is really down there': pepinos-do-mar e a borda da vida; 'how did anyone find out': alguém voltou para olhar, e a conclusão se diz com o porquê e o limite) e os dois títulos ('The deepest point in the Atlantic, about 83 miles off Puerto Rico').
fecho.contra_os_anteriores: Juneau, Los Angeles, a Zona do Canal e o Peru fecharam com 'So', a pergunta repetida, a resposta em lista e uma imagem curta (voz §1). Os dois concorrentes fecham em 'não é a Marianas' (leitura 06). Aqui não há nenhum dos quatro: a última frase é um fato atribuído (F70) dito como imagem de lugar.

inscricao.onde: p5 b2, sobre 'Soon after, a problem with the robot cut this one short.' e a pausa de fim de parágrafo, com o vídeo da NOAA por baixo (registro real, câmera parada).
inscricao.depois_de: on one of a dozen robot dives that expedition made.
inscricao.fala_curta_prevista: Soon after, a problem with the robot cut this one short.
inscricao.posicao_estimada: termina na palavra 1.046 de 2.011 ≈ 5:41 de fala, num vídeo de ≈ 11:20 com a cauda ≈ 50 %: dentro da janela de 35–60 % e fora do 1º minuto (cta §6).
inscricao.por_que: Frase calma, sem número, sem 'here' nem 'this line', sem viagem de câmera nem número-herói, e não é a frase-chave da parte (que é o 'first person' de b6). O rótulo da parede e o crédito da NOAA ocupam o terço de baixo: o regente põe o rótulo em cima ou usa '?lugar=cima' para a peça, nunca as duas placas na mesma faixa (cta §5).
inscricao.reserva: p4 b6, sobre 'They think quakes like that come thousands of years apart.' (≈ 4:59, ≈ 44 %), só com a régua do tempo já parada e o canto de baixo livre; nunca sobre Anegada acendendo nem sobre 1918.
inscricao.nao_ali: o gancho e o 1º minuto; p3 b4–b6 (as placas e a laje animando); p5 b4–b7 (o número e o mergulho); p6 (números em leitura e o anel saltando); p7 b9–b10 (a linha de 60°S).

comentario.onde: p8 b4, sobre as duas primeiras frases ('By NOAA's estimate, no fish lives much deeper than about 27,500 feet. The net that brought up the cusk-eel in 1970 had gone down nearly that far.', ~8 s), sobre o medidor com a faixa da NOAA; a pergunta da abertura já foi respondida em b2–b3. A peça sai antes da última frase, que é a frase-chave, e termina pelo menos 1 s antes da cauda de 20 s (cta §6). Com fala densa no trecho, '?lugar=cima'.
comentario.pergunta: What would you want to see five miles down?
alternativas: Would you dive five miles down, alone?
Would you have gone back to check on the fish?
comentario.por_que: Calma, em segunda pessoa, ligada ao assunto e respondível por quem acabou de ver (cta §7). A principal só oferece uma escolha e pressupõe um fato do vídeo ('five miles down', F03); a 1ª alternativa pressupõe dois (F03, F39), que o verificador confere. Nada de like, inscrição, emoji, 'smash'.
comentario.o_que_o_roteirista_faz: Deixa as duas frases de b4 antes da última calmas e sem número novo além do da NOAA. Quem fecha a pergunta e a roda no 'node marca/cta/pecas/_perguntas.mjs --q="…"' é o redator-de-tela; a mesma pergunta vai à descrição e ao comentário fixado. A chamada é só de tela: a voz não a lê. O motor sem rosto monta as chamadas a seu modo: a Sala confere como ele as recebe; se não houver trecho antes da cauda, a tela final à esquerda volta ao Lucas (cta §6).

About 83 miles off Puerto Rico, a U.S. island, lies the deepest point in the Atlantic Ocean. It's more than five miles down. Stand Mount Everest on the bottom, and its top 1,500 feet would stick out of the water. When you think "deepest ocean," you think Mariana. But that's the Pacific, about 9,500 miles away.

In 1964, a French crew dove into the Puerto Rico Trench and reported a crowd of fish. In 2019, a submersible went back to the exact same spot. It found no fish at all. The first person to reach the deepest point itself got there only in December 2018. And for decades, the official list of undersea features gave that point a number about 1,200 feet too deep, even after sonar showed otherwise. So what is really down there, and how did anyone find out? You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of the bottom of the Atlantic begins.

On January 27, 1883, a steamer of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, the Blake, lowered a weighted wire into the sea north of Puerto Rico. Its commander was a Navy officer named Brownson, who had taken charge of the ship a few months earlier. The wire went down more than five miles before it touched bottom. That was about 60 miles east of the deepest point the sonar would later find.

It came back up with a sample of the seafloor and a reading of the water temperature down there. The survey's report for that year describes the bottom as brown ooze. At the time, that was believed to be the greatest depth a sample had ever been brought up from.

The trench itself had been found eight years earlier, by the British research ship HMS Challenger, under Captain Nares, far to the east. Its sounding there reached about 23,000 feet. The trench runs for hundreds of miles, almost parallel to Puerto Rico's north coast.

In 1939, the cruiser USS Milwaukee bounced sound off the bottom north of Puerto Rico. It reported more than 28,000 feet, a record for the Atlantic at the time. The spot was named the Milwaukee Deep, after the ship. That summer, newspapers printed the news in a bulletin from the National Geographic Society.

A sound could give a number. It couldn't show anyone what was down there.

In 1964, people went down into the trench themselves. They rode in a French bathyscaphe, a deep-diving craft, called Archimède. It went more than four miles down. Exactly how deep, the sources disagree. It never reached the deepest point, though.

About 24,000 feet down, the French crew reported a crowd of fish. Some 200 of them, along about a mile of seafloor. Their account, published the next year, described them as snailfish, a family of fish. Keep those fish in mind.

In 1970, by the account of NOAA, the U.S. ocean and weather agency, a net hauled up from the trench brought back a small cusk-eel. A cusk-eel is a fish shaped like an eel, and this one was about eight inches long. The net had gone down nearly as deep as the deepest point of the Atlantic. No one knows, though, how deep the fish was when it swam in.

A crew could see only a small patch of the trench, and a net could only bring something up. Neither could map the floor. That took a different kind of sonar.

In 2002 and 2003, the U.S. Geological Survey mapped the trench with multibeam sonar, a ship's sonar that maps the seafloor in a wide strip. It took three cruises on a NOAA ship. By the end, those surveys showed the deepest part of the trench at about 27,300 feet. That was 15 years before anyone reached the deepest point.

Why is the trench so deep? Along it, two of Earth's plates, the giant slabs of its outer shell, mostly slide past each other, with only a little of one sinking under the other. The Caribbean plate moves east about three-quarters of an inch a year.

By the USGS's measure, the trench has the most negative gravity anomaly on Earth. Gravity there falls further below normal than anywhere else. The agency found a tilted slab of limestone that starts more than 4,000 feet above sea level. It ends about 13,000 feet below it. And it reads rotated blocks of rock deep in the trench as signs that the trench has been sinking.

On the trench's walls, its maps showed something else.

The USGS says those walls show many old underwater landslides, and that the risk of a landslide tsunami appears to be high.

In October 1918, an earthquake struck the Mona Passage, west of Puerto Rico. It wasn't in the trench. NOAA's tsunami database puts it at magnitude 7.1. Its tsunami ran as high as 20 feet up Puerto Rico's west coast. The quake and its tsunami killed more than 100 people.

Farther east, an island holds a sign of what the trench itself can do. Anegada is a low, flat island in the British Virgin Islands. Hundreds of coral boulders lie far inland there, along about six miles of its north shore, the side that faces the trench. Dating the coral by its uranium, a 2025 study placed the tsunami that left them sometime between 1381 and 1391. That's about a century before Columbus reached the Caribbean. The authors suspect the coral died in summer or fall.

The earthquake behind it struck the eastern part of this trench, far from its deepest point. Computer models put it at magnitude 8 or more. The scientists who dated the coral call it the only known sign that this stretch of the trench can do that. And it wasn't behind the deadly tsunami of 1918. They think quakes like that come thousands of years apart.

To see the trench's walls, you need a camera down there.

In 2015, a NOAA robot filmed the trench's south wall, almost 20,000 feet down. That's in the eastern part of the trench, a long way from its deepest point. The robot, Deep Discoverer, worked from NOAA's ship Okeanos Explorer, on one of a dozen robot dives that expedition made. Soon after, a problem with the robot cut this one short.

In December 2018, the Five Deeps Expedition mapped the trench with a modern sonar. To get the sonar right, the ship lowered instruments to measure how fast sound travels at every depth, from the surface to the floor. Most of the seafloor it covered had been mapped before.

By the expedition's survey, the deepest point of the Atlantic is about 27,500 feet down. Give or take about 16 feet. The scientists give that margin with 95 percent confidence. They built their map as a grid of squares about 250 feet across. The results were published in 2021. That point lies about 83 miles from the nearest coast of Puerto Rico, off Aguadilla, in the island's northwest. More than three million people live in Puerto Rico.

On Wednesday, December 19, 2018, Victor Vescovo took a submersible called Limiting Factor down to the spot the sonar had just mapped. He made the trip alone, in a sub built to reach the bottom of any ocean. The trip down took about two and a half hours. He was the first person to reach the deepest point of the Atlantic. The sub's own gauges confirmed the sonar's number, within about 7 feet.

That number was not the one in the official list.

Until at least 2019, the official list of undersea features had the Milwaukee Deep at about 28,700 feet. That's almost exactly what the newspapers reported in 1939. The floor the sonar found is about 1,200 feet shallower. And U.S. government sonar had shown a shallower floor since 2003. As late as 2011, a press release for a planned deep-diving sub listed more than 28,000 feet.

In 2019, two scientists, Heather Stewart and Alan Jamieson, checked the published depths against sonar data that was already public. In their check, the real floor came out shallower every time. They wrote that numbers like these had spread, uncorrected, through online sources and the scientific literature. At the spot the old listing pointed to, their study found about 24,400 feet, the top of a ridge.

Their study also put the deepest point somewhere else. Working from public data from eight older surveys, it placed that point about 36 miles west of the sonar's spot, in waters claimed by the Dominican Republic. Their study came out before the expedition's own results. Those were published in 2021, and they placed the deepest point in U.S. waters off Puerto Rico, about 100 miles from the Dominican Republic.

As of October 2026, the international list of undersea feature names no longer includes the Milwaukee Deep. The two scientists had asked for that name to fall out of use. The expedition's scientists write that it handed all of its sonar data to Seabed 2030, the project to map the whole ocean floor by 2030.

The expedition also took its sonar, and its sub, to the other end of the Atlantic.

The other contender is the South Sandwich Trench, in the far South Atlantic, where one plate dives under another about three inches a year. That is three to four times the pace of the plates off Puerto Rico. The islands there are a chain of small volcanoes, with no one living on them. Both Britain and Argentina claim them. In August 2026, a Landsat satellite caught the heat of a lava lake in the crater of Mount Michael, one of those volcanoes. A 2021 study calls this trench the coldest known ecosystem in the deep trenches.

The expedition mapped this trench with its sonar in 2019. Before that, about nine-tenths of it had never been mapped. The depth most often published for its deepest point, a 2019 study found, was deeper than the sonar's number for Puerto Rico. The sonar settled that. Its deepest point, the Meteor Deep, is about 370 feet shallower than the one off Puerto Rico. The expedition mapped it but didn't dive there.

The name Meteor Deep is old, after a German research ship. Since 2021, it has officially belonged to the spot the sonar found, about 30 miles from where older books put it. The expedition had wanted to call it Pressure Deep, after its own ship, the Pressure Drop.

In 2023, the International Hydrographic Organization recognized the Southern Ocean. It begins at 60 degrees south. The organization says the line carries no political meaning, and not every country uses it. Argentina, for one, disagrees. By that line, the Meteor Deep, well to the north, is in the Atlantic. The trench's southern tip crosses the line. Just south of the line lies the deepest point of the Southern Ocean, the Factorian Deep. The Limiting Factor reached its bottom in 2019, and that's where the odd name comes from. Its neighbor, about 20 miles away, got the other half of the name: Limiting Deep.

Off Puerto Rico, the French crew's fish were waiting for a second look.

In 2019, the same sub went back to the spot where the French crew had reported their fish. It was the craft that had carried Victor Vescovo to the deepest point the year before. Where the French had counted about 200 fish, it found none. It found sea cucumbers instead, about as many as the fish the French had counted. From the outside, the two look a lot alike: similar color, similar texture, similar shape.

The scientists who went back concluded that the "fish" of 1964 were sea cucumbers. It's a conclusion drawn from the count and the look. The animals the French saw that day can't be checked again.

By NOAA's estimate, no fish lives much deeper than about 27,500 feet. The net that brought up the cusk-eel in 1970 had gone down nearly that far. The deepest point in the Atlantic, about 83 miles off Puerto Rico, sits right at that edge.
